name: Insects in medicine

lead: Insects in medicine, or entomotherapy, covers the therapeutic use of whole insects and products such as venom, honey, silk and larvae. Traditions in Egypt, Greece, Rome, China and elsewhere list insect remedies for wounds, skin lesions and inflammation, and one modern form, maggot debridement therapy, is a regulated medical procedure.

The appearance link is through skin and wound healing: cleaner wounds and ulcers heal with less tissue damage, and traditional systems used insect preparations on skin conditions. Research is strongest for maggot therapy in chronic wounds and exploratory for venom peptides and other compounds.

paras: In clinics, sterile larvae of the green bottle fly (Lucilia sericata) are placed in a wound under dressings for a few days to remove dead tissue. Traditional systems use powders, decoctions, poultices or stings. Honey dressings are a separate, widely used insect product.

Maggot therapy needs moist wounds with adequate oxygen and can be disliked by patients; stings and venom products can trigger allergic reactions, and unregulated whole-insect remedies carry contamination risks.

chain: Insect products clean or treat wounds and inflamed skin
Wounds heal faster with less necrotic tissue
angle.text: Insect-derived treatments are relevant to appearance through wound and skin healing, for example clinical maggot therapy for ulcers and traditional insect preparations for skin lesions.

lead: Entomotherapy is the use of insects and their derivatives for healing. Grokipedia describes more than 235 insect species from 15 orders used worldwide, mostly for skin disorders, digestive complaints, inflammation and infections [1]. Documented uses range from Egyptian and Roman texts to the Bencao Gangmu, the 16th-century Chinese materia medica, which lists dozens of insect remedies [1].

The appearance-related thread is wound and skin care. Maggot debridement therapy, in which sterilised fly larvae clean dead tissue from non-healing wounds, is authorised by the US FDA as a prescription-only medical device since 2004 [2]. Honey, silk-derived materials and bee venom are other insect products discussed for skin and inflammatory conditions [1].

paras: The practice includes applying live insects (maggots, stinging bees), using secretions such as venom and honey, and preparing powders or decoctions from silkworms, beetles and ants [1]. Traditional Chinese medicine records remedies from silkworm pupae and bee venom for convulsions and arthritis [1].

Maggots have reportedly been used on wounds since antiquity; Napoleon's surgeon Dominique Larrey noted during the 1798-1801 Egypt and Syria campaign that some fly larvae ate only dead tissue, and Civil War doctor J.F. Zacharias wrote that they cleaned wounds better than available agents [2]. After World War I, William S. Baer used maggot therapy at Boston Children's Hospital [2]. Pliny the Elder recorded many insect remedies in his Naturalis Historia [1].

Larvae secrete proteolytic enzymes that liquefy necrotic tissue and are thought to have antimicrobial effects, including activity against MRSA in laboratory studies; the most common species is Lucilia sericata [2]. In January 2004 the FDA allowed marketing of maggots as prescription-only devices for non-healing necrotic wounds [2]. Dressings are designed to contain the larvae and reduce the tickling sensation [2].

A 2014 systematic review found maggot therapy improves healing in chronic ulcers, with tentative evidence for diabetic foot ulcers [2]. A Cochrane review found maggot debridement broadly as effective as other methods for venous leg ulcers, with poor-quality data [2]. Studies of venom peptides and edible-insect extracts are mostly laboratory or animal research [1].

Wounds must be moist with adequate oxygen for maggot therapy, and some patients find it distasteful [2]. Venom-based and whole-insect folk uses carry allergic reaction risk, and regulatory hurdles and cultural stigma limit adoption [1].
